title: The hypertrophy series: determining the optimal workout length
summary: NH explains how to decide when a session should end using his baseline concept: stop once the muscles trained that day can no longer move weights relevant to the absolute intensity set by the opening strength work. Sessions should be as short as possible, lengthen with advancement, and a mature program keeps the set brackets stable while tonnage rises vertically.
claims: A session should be as short as possible; cram all the necessary work into the smallest time span
The more advanced you get, the less you can rely on intensity, so you add sets and frequency, which adds time; programming must waste no second
Short does not mean minimalist: keep plenty of accessories and variations, but program them intelligently within maximum recoverable volume
End the session when the muscles you train can no longer return to a baseline relevant to the absolute intensity established by the opening strength work
If you squat 300 lb for your strength work and later find yourself doing a squat variation with 150 lb, you have dug too deep and should have gone home
Sessions get longer as you advance; a novice training two hours is doing junk volume and can get by with 40-minute sessions
Never let anyone call your sessions too short or too long as long as they produce progression
The aim of training is to damage the fibers so they cannot return to a relevant baseline; you can never fully destroy the baseline short of injury
Maximum recoverable volume can only be diagnosed after the fact, so he prefers the in-session baseline cue; most people do not overshoot and should not be anxious about it
Once you have established the baseline for a given day, it barely fluctuates, so you do not need to recalculate it every session
Progression should be slow: the set brackets stay stationary while weights inside them rise; you only add sets or frequency when adding weight is no longer realistic
A perfect program has an immovable baseline and grows vertically in tonnage rather than horizontally by adding sets and days
Watching the baseline within the relevant intensity window prevents junk volume; with practice judging it becomes second nature
